t: Grid Teleportation Traversal — BFS with Letter-Level Teleport Expansion
o: Find minimum moves from (0,0) to (m−1,n−1) on a grid with obstacles and portals. Moving costs 1; stepping onto an unused portal letter lets you jump (for free) to any other cell with that letter, and each letter works at most once. Because teleports are free, this is a 0-weight-edge shortest-path problem solvable with plain BFS: when you first reach any cell of letter L, immediately enqueue every cell of letter L at the same distance and mark L consumed. In Example 1, teleporting from (0,0) to (1,1) before moving gives distance 2.
k: Teleportation is zero-cost, so treat all cells sharing a letter as one supernode expanded on first visit
Each letter expands at most once, giving O(mn) total work despite many portal cells
Standard BFS layer order still yields correct distances since 0-weight jumps happen within the same layer

a.n: Approach 1: BFS with one-time letter expansion
a.i: Run ordinary BFS by distance layers. When dequeuing (or enqueuing) a cell holding letter L not yet used, mark L used and push all cells containing L at the current distance. Since the jump adds no moves, these cells belong to the same BFS layer, so FIFO order preserves correctness. Each cell enters the queue at most once, and each letter triggers at most one scan of its positions.
s: Precompute pos[L] = list of cells with letter L.
BFS from (0,0); when visiting a cell with unused letter L, mark L used and enqueue all pos[L] cells with dist+0.
Relax the four neighbors normally with dist+1.
Return dist at (m−1,n−1), or −1 if unreachable.
a.t: O(mn) time — each cell is enqueued at most once and each of the 26 letters expands its cell list once.
a.sp: O(mn) for distances and the queue, plus O(mn) worst case for portal position lists.

w: Use the BFS-with-expansion approach — it is optimal and simple. Using a deque (push front for free teleports, back for normal moves) makes the 0-weight handling obvious; a plain queue also works if teleports are processed when the cell is dequeued. Pitfalls: reusing a letter twice, teleporting onto obstacle cells (letters never sit on '#'), and forgetting the destination might itself be a portal. Follow-ups: weighted moves (switch to Dijkstra/0-1 BFS), limited teleport uses per letter, or counting shortest paths.
